title: NVIDIA opens three Nemotron 3.5 Parse datasets and a fine-tuning recipe; DFlash2 inference is 7.62x faster
summary: If you're using models to turn scans, PDFs, or charts into structured data, NVIDIA has now opened up Nemotron 3.5 Parse's training data and fine-tuning recipe, plus a DFlash2 acceleration option: on a single H200, throughput at concurrency 1 jumps 7.62x.
ai_summary: Following the release of Nemotron 3.5 Parse, NVIDIA is open-sourcing three things: three synthetic training datasets (9.98M charts, 1M tables, 7.9M multilingual OCR examples), an SFT+RLVR fine-tuning recipe, and a speculative-decoding accelerator called DFlash2. Training starts with supervised fine-tuning to learn page reading, then uses reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards to improve consistency: loop-flagged outputs drop from 126 pages to 29, and the overall score rises from 66.24 to 71.38. On a single H200 in BF16, DFlash2 improves throughput 7.62x at concurrency 1 and reaches 20.44 pages/s at concurrency 512. The most practical part is applying the recipe to your own documents: in NVIDIA's example, dental-form first-attempt success goes from 0.00% to 96.58%. These are NVIDIA's own evaluation numbers, so validate them on your data.
brief: The three open datasets cover 9.98M chart examples, 1M table examples, and 7.9M multilingual OCR pages, and include images, labels, and training formats.
In a matched comparison, RLVR drops loop-flagged outputs from 126 pages to 29 and lifts the overall score from 66.24 to 71.38.
On a single H200 in BF16, DFlash2 delivers 7.62x throughput at concurrency 1 and reaches 20.44 pages/s at concurrency 512.
Dental-form fine-tuning example: first-attempt success rises from 0.00% to 96.58%; the recipe is open and can be applied to your own documents.

cover.headline: Nemotron Parse opens up further
cover.highlight: Open data, a fine-tuning recipe, and faster inference

sections.h: What it is: turning a page into structured data with labels and bounding boxes

blocks.p: Nemotron 3.5 Parse is NVIDIA's document parsing model: give it a scanned page or PDF image, and it arranges the page content in reading order, labels each block by category (heading, paragraph, table, chart, etc.), and returns a bounding box—the rectangle coordinates that locate that content on the page. Tables and charts are also converted into structured records for downstream RAG (retrieval-augmented generation: pull relevant content from documents, then let the model answer) or for agents.

The blog adds three things after the model release: the synthetic datasets used for training, a reusable fine-tuning recipe, and DFlash2 for faster inference. The emphasis is on opening both the data and the method, so others can train their own document models along the same path.

sections.h: Which three datasets are being released?

blocks.p: All three datasets are synthetic: instead of manually labeling real scans, they are generated by programmatically rendering charts, tables, and multilingual pages. Because every bar's value and every cell's content is known at generation time, the ground truth is naturally exact, and it's easy to vary fonts, layouts, and languages to expand diversity.

blocks.p: Each dataset includes images, labels, generation documentation, and the training format. The authors suggest using them to fine-tune a document model directly, or following the same method to generate new variants for a particular document type or language.
The community has already extended Parse to Thai, Persian/Farsi, and Arabic; this release of data and recipes is meant to help more people do similar work.

sections.h: Why chart and table parsing improved

blocks.p: This release's most visible gains are in charts and tables, especially hard, ambiguous cases. Many bar and line charts have no numbers printed at all; the model has to read the axes and bar heights to infer values. The announcement gives one example: Parse recovered 18, 27, 39, and 54 from a chart's geometry.

Tables are trickier because structure is meaning: if a row or column shifts, the interpretation of the whole table changes. These gains come mainly from synthetic data—render charts and tables with known ground truth, then have the model reverse the process, like working from a controlled workbook.

callout.title: Why synthetic data is especially well suited to charts and tables
callout.text: Labeling real documents by hand is slow, expensive, and error-prone; with rendered images, every bar value and every cell is known, so you can automatically generate large numbers of examples with ground truth.

sections.h: Two-stage training: SFT teaches the capability, RLVR improves consistency

blocks.p: Training has two steps. The first is SFT (supervised fine-tuning): the model gets paired page + standard structured output data and learns to read a page and represent its contents. This stage covers text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents, building the foundational capability.

The second is RLVR (reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards), with GRPO as the optimization algorithm. The model samples outputs, and automatically checkable rules score them: did the chart recover the correct series and values, is the structure usable, is the same content being generated repeatedly. A hard page can have multiple valid representations, so the approach doesn't force a single correct answer—instead it rewards correct and complete output and penalizes looping and unfinished output.

fig.title: RLVR reduces loops, cuts overlong outputs, and raises the total score
fig.subtitle: Development checkpoints: matched SFT vs. GRPO comparison; amber shows GRPO values
fig.note: These are development checkpoints, not the final released model; loop counts use a repetition check.

blocks.p: The announcement provides a matched comparison: loop-flagged outputs fall from 126 pages to 29, roughly 77% fewer; outputs hitting the 9,000-token limit fall from 185 pages to 35; the total score rises from 66.24 to 71.38, including +5.18 points for tables and +4.15 points for charts. Note that these are development checkpoints, not the final released model.

sections.h: DFlash2 makes inference faster: architecture changes plus a small model that guesses first

blocks.p: A parsing model has to produce a lot of text and structure for every page, so it is compute-hungry. Parse 3.5 changes four parts of the architecture, shown below next to Parse 2.0.

fig.title: Parse 3.5 replaces the fixed canvas with page-adaptive inputs
fig.subtitle: Amber shows what changed

items.label: Visual tokens compressed into a prefix

blocks.p: The most interesting part is speculative decoding: a small draft model first guesses what comes next, then the main model verifies those guesses in one shot; correct guesses save time. The built-in MTP head only looks ahead 1 token; DFlash2 is a stronger draft model that guesses up to 32 tokens ahead, and Parse verifies them together. In the measured 32-token configuration, it accepts about 14 draft tokens on average, plus the target token, for roughly 15 output tokens of progress per verification step.

On a single H200 in BF16, using the same benchmark of 2,078 pages: at concurrency 1, DFlash2 improves throughput 7.62x; at concurrency 512, it improves it 1.52x. In absolute terms at concurrency 512, Parse 3.5 without speculation is 13.48 pages/s, with DFlash2 it is 20.44 pages/s, and Parse 2.0 is only 2.98 pages/s. That puts them at 4.53x and 6.86x relative to Parse 2.0.

fig.title: At concurrency 512, DFlash2 lifts throughput from 13.48 to 20.44 pages/s
fig.subtitle: Units: pages/s; one H200, BF16, same 2,078 pages; amber shows DFlash2

sections.h: When one pass isn't enough, double or triple pass re-reads hard regions

blocks.p: With faster inference, there is room to re-read difficult regions. Single pass reads the whole page once and outputs text, layout, tables, and charts. Double pass crops the table and chart regions found in the first pass, zooms in and re-parses them, then merges the refinements back. Triple pass adds a detection mode pass to confirm that all bounding boxes are found and no text has been missed, then re-reads the charts and tables it found.

fig.title: If one pass isn't enough, crop the hard regions and read again
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: amber shows the additional stages in multi-pass parsing; scores come from NVIDIA's published reference evaluation

items.label: Outputs text, layout, tables, and charts in one go
Double: crop table and chart regions, zoom in, and re-read
Triple: add detection mode to verify boxes and text

blocks.p: In NVIDIA's published reference evaluation, double pass adds 2.18 ParseBench points over single pass, and triple pass adds 2.46 points. The cost is that multiple crops lead to multiple requests and lower throughput—essentially trading speed for accuracy on hard regions.

callout.title: Speed and quality can be tuned separately
callout.text: DFlash2 solves the speed problem; double/triple pass solves accuracy on hard regions. They can be combined: use multi-pass parsing to raise quality first, then use DFlash2 to recover the extra compute.

sections.h: Fine-tuning recipe: a dental form example shows how to use it

blocks.p: NVIDIA's recipe is a pipeline: use your own image-plus-standard-label pairs, run SFT with NeMo Automodel, then run GRPO reinforcement learning with NeMo RL, using vLLM to generate candidate answers. You also need a verifier to judge whether each extraction is correct. The included document reward components cover text fidelity, bounding boxes, tables, chart facts, and completion; you can combine the components relevant to your task and add your own schema checks.

The example uses a synthetic dental form containing an odontogram (a chart showing teeth, planned procedures, and affected tooth surfaces). Before fine-tuning, Parse can read the printed tooth numbers but misses the planned procedure table; after SFT, it learns to associate each marked tooth with a procedure and position. The original figure says all six chart rows match the target after SFT.

In the evaluation on 256 held-out forms from the same generator, with 8 samples per page, estimated first-attempt success (sampled pass@1, meaning the first sample is exactly correct) rises from 0.00% for the base model to 95.85% after SFT and 96.58% after RLVR. Success is defined as: natural completion, chart content exactly matching, and normalized page text with no errors.

fig.title: Dental form: first-attempt success from 0 to 96.58%
fig.subtitle: 256 held-out forms, 8 samples per page; success = completion + matching chart + error-free text; unit: %

list: The license details for the three datasets and the recipe aren't listed separately; check the corresponding model and dataset pages before using them in practice.
The fine-tuning results are only demonstrated on synthetic data; the dental example itself comes from the same synthetic generator, so performance on real, heterogeneous scans is unknown.
DFlash2 throughput was only measured on a single H200 in BF16; other GPUs, precisions, and higher concurrency aren't covered.
Double/triple pass only gets score improvements (+2.18, +2.46); no numbers are given for how many extra requests or how much throughput is lost.
Pricing isn't mentioned: the model and datasets are open, but you have to calculate your own GPU costs for self-hosted inference.

blocks.p: The value: if you want to turn scans, PDFs, invoices, medical records, or forms into structured data, this open data and recipe can save you from reinventing the wheel; chart parsing, table parsing, and multilingual OCR all have ready starting points. DFlash2's 7.62x gain at concurrency 1 is more noticeable than at high concurrency.

The cost: you need to prepare paired data, write a verifier, and run training yourself. The evaluation numbers in the post come from NVIDIA's own benchmarks and development checkpoints, not a universal guarantee.

list: If you're building a RAG system or document agent: start with Parse 3.5 as-is, see if it is good enough, then decide whether to fine-tune.
If you have a specific format (dental forms, invoices, contracts): follow the recipe with SFT + RLVR; it's easier than training from scratch.
If you're low-concurrency, processing one page at a time: enable DFlash2 first; at high-concurrency batch processing the gain is smaller, but it's still faster than Parse 2.0.
If documents are hard (dense tables, small charts): use double or triple pass and trade throughput for accuracy.
